Legal technicalities AKA due process, complete with Latin phrases can often seem arcane to the layman, but they are key to understanding the system that holds the power of life and death over all citizens.

Certainly, the police and the courts have to have a degree of discretion in choosing what laws to enforce and when, but they can never be allowed to choose which laws to obey. That has been a serious problem with the implementation of Prop 215 in California, one of the earliest challenges being the Kubby case.
See
 California Narks Lie to Justify Disobeying Prop 215. And They Lie About Me In The Process.
and
 The Rule of Lawlessness: Police Brazenness In The Kubby Case.
The Fourth And Fifth Amendments, Or Forfeiture and Thievery. The Choice Is Ours.
and links

Now the Kubby case is heating up again, in both California and Canada.

There are Kubby press releases below. The first describes how fraud was used to obtain the search warrant that allowed the police to search the Kubbys home. Obviously, if the search was invalid, there would be no case at all.

It is quite clear now that the Placer County police and the North Tahoe Narcotics Task Force knew that they were committing fraud on the court in obtaining the warrant. Contrary to their claims, they knew that there was no DEA file identifying a journalist as a Jamaican drug dealer.
See
 Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report May 2, 2005 Drug Czar Imports Scottish Expert Who Says Cannabis As Big A Threat As Heroin. Scotland A Mess. Interview With Steve Kubby About His Case

Nonetheless, the Judge declined to overturn the verdicts even though, as noted below, Placer County authorities have never furnished a copy of the alleged report, nor have they ever denied the allegations of fraud.

What have the facts got to do with it?

Although the Kubbys can and will appeal the Judge's ruling, there has been another discovery of enormous importance.

The first judge in the Kubby case, Superior Court Judge James L. Roeder was so clearly biased that the Kubbys demanded that he recuse himself. He had attempted to  prevent the Kubbys from even mentioning Prop 215 in their defense in a California state court!

Michelle Kubby wrote, Honorable Judge Roeder of the Placer County Court, before whom the above-entitled cases are currently pending, is prejudiced or biased against me or my interests whereby I cannot be afforded a fair and impartial trial before such judge. Wherefore, affiant moves for the peremptory disqualification of said Judge.

Perhaps Roeder realized that he had committed a reversible error, but he did agree to let another judge handle the case, and formally recused himself.
(Recuse: to disqualify (oneself) as judge in a particular case; broadly : to remove (oneself) from participation to avoid a conflict of interest Merriam-Webster) 

Obviously, once a judge is recused, he is out of the case permanently and is not supposed to be involved again. So that should have been the last we would hear from him in this matter, and as far as anyone knew, it was until now.

A little background:
During the search the police claimed to have found an unusably small quantity of psilocybin mushroom and peyote cactus in a canister in a drawer in the guest bedroom. Inasmuch as Steve has written a book on psychedelics it is plausible but unproven that they belong to him, but here is where is gets weird.  

He was not convicted of possession the natural substances which the police claimed to have found, but of possession of psilocyn and mescaline, the active ingredients which the police extracted in their lab.
See
 A Critique of the Kubby Refugee Ruling: What Is It About Dead That You Don't Understand?
and
 Prosecutor Demands That Kubby Be Jailed to Die Without Medical Marijuana; Judge Agrees, But Jailer Refuses to Commit Murder. Just When You Thought They Couldn't Get Any Crazier

The jury had originally voted to acquit, but reversed itself and voted to convict on these charges after having the legal definition of a usable quantity re-read to them. The problem with that was that the police had manufactured the usable substances by extracting them from their natural sources.
See
 Kubby Trial Ends. Jury Split Eleven to One for Acquittal on Marijuana Charges. Prosecution's Arbitrary Limits on the Number of Plants Fails. Significance for the Rest of California.

Steve Kubby himself was not too worried. He said, The other charges are unfortunate, but we'll deal with that issue at the appropriate time." At the time, I wrote, These other charges pose no real threat to Steve. Wrong!

These were very minor misdemeanors should have resulted in nothing more than a fine and unsupervised probation, instead they were used in an attempt to kill Steve. There is no other way to put. They knew first hand what had happened to him when they locked him up following his arrest.
See
 Judge Releases Kubbys On Own Recognizance.
Libertarian Party Organizations Now Committed To The Marijuana Issue.
Large Number Of Plants Will Force Dealing With Difficult Questions
-- Analysis By Richard Cowan

When it became clear that the misdemeanors would not accomplish the goal of silencing Kubby, despite the tiny amounts involved and all of the problems with the case, there was a move by the State to have the conviction converted to a felony!

Now, there are serious legal questions about converting such a misdemeanor to a felony, but we can leave that for another time. The real scandal almost went undiscovered and was just found by former Auburn Journal Editor, Pat McCartney.
See
 Local Editor Says Kubby Prosecution Ends with a Whimper.

When Steve appealed the conviction, the Placer County court clerk inquired as to whether it should be handled as a felony or a misdemeanor. She sent the inquiry to Judge Roeder, who should have sent it back with the notation that he had recused himself.

Instead, he wrote on the form, Process As Felony Appeal and signed it. Moreover, there is also a document from the Appeals Court stating, Judge Roeder ordered this to be processed as a felony 

The immediate consequence of it being treated as a felony was that Steve Kubby would need to appear personally in order for the appeal to be heard, which would not have been the case if it was a misdemeanor. At that point he was called a fugitive, even though he had originally gone to Canada with the permission of the Court.

Consequently, Judge Roeder and by extension the Appeals Court violated a fundamental rule in both the appearance and practice of justice. Presumably, at some point the cumulative weight of all the violations of the Kubbys rights may even become too much for the State of California, and they will eventually prevail.

In the meantime, however, Canada is doing its best to send them back to California before that happens, and this latest discovery is very important in that process.

Canada claims that Steve Kubby is inadmissible because he was convicted of a felony, which he was not. Then, because he could not risk going to California to appeal his felony conviction (according to Roeder's order) and die in jail, Canada also said he was a fugitive, which he was not because as noted he had come here with the permission of the court that had convicted him of a misdemeanor, not a felony. These new revelations will be a key part of the Kubbys Pre-Removal Risk Assessment, which is a key part of the Canadian refugee (bureaucratic) process.

I have been following this case closely from the beginning and it is turning out to be a major legal scandal that demands that the California Bar Association and anyone who cares about justice must confront. Canada would rather not have to admit that the criminal justice system in DEAland is seriously flawed, but this latest twist makes it hard to deny the sad truth.

 PLACER COUNTY JUDGE DENIES REDRESS FOR PROSECUTORIAL FRAUD IN KUBBY CASE

 For a second time, a Placer County judge has denied the request of exiled medical-marijuana activist Steve Kubby to overturn his conviction because of frauds committed by the prosecution.

At a hearing held Monday in the historic Auburn courthouse, Judge John L. Cosgrove declined to reconsider his May 16 decision to deny a new hearing based on a writ of error coram nobis.

The writ alleges that Placer County authorities relied on a fraudulent DEA document to obtain the search warrant that led to the Jan. 19, 1999, arrest of Steve and Michele Kubby at their Olympic Valley home.
(MarijuanaNews note: From http://www.civil-liberties.com/living/part6.html:
A motion in nature of Coram Nobis can be filed in the court that sentenced the defendant but would be limited to correcting errors of the most fundamental character to achieve justice where no other remedy is available. The action is authorized pursuant to the All Writs Act, (28 USC #1651(a)), and would be of the same general character as one that would be a ground for relief under 28 USC #2255 for Habeas Corpus. US v Morgan, 346 US 502 (1954). 

At Monday's hearing, McPike called the prosecutor's appeal a collateral attack on probation. California law precludes such an appeal process and requires prosecutors to file a writ in order to appeal a probation order whether or not a custodial sentence has been imposed.

So, the Appellate Court was wrong in hearing this? Judge Cosgrove asked.

That's my conclusion, McPike said.

It's a tantalizing thought to agree with you, Cosgrove commented.

Deputy District Attorney Chris Cattran said at Mondays hearing that jurisdiction over the Kubby case remains in the appellate court. He also noted the absence of Kubby, who has lived in British Columbia since the spring of 2001. Felony proceedings typically require the presence of the defendant.

McPike argued that only a writ of error coram nobis in the original jurisdiction could untangle what he called a highly unusual procedure that followed Kubby's conviction.

Afterward, McPike explained what happened:
There is a statutory 30 days under Penal Code 1466. The DA was actually beyond the 30 days. Also, any appeal may not be made IF it challenges a Judge's discretionary grant of probation. Kubby was in fact granted probation so the appellate court had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal filed over 60 days after the grant of misdemeanor probation. We contend that the appeal is void and Steve Kubby is protected by law from having his conviction raised to a felony.

Speaking from his Sun Peak residence, Steve Kubby said the decision was not a surprise.

A judge can turn your life upside down with the stroke of a pen, yet that same judge will come up with endless reasons why they don't have the power to fix the mess they helped to create Kubby said.

The writ of error coram nobis charges that in its 1999 Statement of Probable Cause, Placer County authorities used a purported DEA report identifying journalist Pete Brady as a Jamaican drug smuggler. Brady, who was observed visiting the Kubbys during a six-month investigation, later attempted to obtain a copy of the N.A.D.I.S. report, but was informed that no such report existed. Placer County authorities have never furnished a copy of the alleged report, nor have they ever denied the allegations of fraud. 

After the North Tahoe Narcotics Task Force searched the Kubby residence, Placer County charged the couple with 19 felony counts. A jury acquitted Michele Kubby of all charges and acquitted Steve Kubby of the marijuana charges against him, but convicted him of misdemeanor possession of peyote and a piece of psilocybin mushroom stem.

(I)t must be presumed that the People were fully cognizant of their position, rights and obligations both in respect to the Criminal Law and the Rules of Professional Responsibility as those rules relate to prosecutors in governmental service, McPike asserts. The factual situation is that the Court of Appeal would not have rendered any judgment had it not been imposed upon to act contrary to statute.

We've accused them of fraud and they're not denying it, Kubby said.Next we find out that their bogus appeal, that they say makes me an alleged 'felony fugitive,' was a fraud.  Now we learn that a disqualified judge snuck back into this case in order to illegally and willfully harm me and the medical marijuana movement.

report, but was informed that no such report existed. Placer County authorities have never furnished a copy of the alleged report, nor have they ever denied the allegations of fraud.

JUDGE ROEDER'S ILLEGAL ORDER TO MAKE STEVE A 'FELONY FUGITIVE'

Now online at http://www.kubby.com/Placer/Roeder.html is the secret document that none of us saw until recently. Only because of the persistent efforts of former Auburn Journal Editor, Pat McCartney, were we ever able to learn about it.

This photo copy of an internal legal decision shows Judge James  Roeder being asked to rule if the Placer County DA's appeal should be entered as a misdemeanor or felony appeal.  Although previously  disqualified from having anything to do with our case, Judge Roeder willfully and fraudulently ruled that the appeal of Steve's misdemeanor sentence and probation should be entered as a felony appeal.
